title: Mithras and Pythagoras
bigQuestion: How can we learn about a secret group that left almost no writing of its own?

story.title: The Last Day of the Dig
story.kicker: On the final day of a dig in London, a face from the Roman world comes up out of the mud.
paragraphs: It is September 1954 in London. The city is still rebuilding after World War II. On a street called Walbrook, builders plan a big new office building. Before they pour concrete, a team of archaeologists gets a short time to dig.

The team is led by W. F. Grimes and Audrey Williams. Deep in the ground, they have found the walls of a small Roman building. It is long and narrow, with a rounded end. Saturday, 18 September, is supposed to be the last day of the dig.

Then someone on the team sees something pale in the dark, wet mud. They lift it out with care. It is a marble head of a young man. He wears a soft cap that folds forward at the top. His face looks calm. He has been buried for about 1,700 years.

The news spreads fast. Long lines of Londoners come to see the old building. The head belongs to Mithras, a god that some Romans worshipped in secret. People start to ask: who met in this small, dark room? And what did they do there?
story.think: The team almost missed the head because it was the last day. What does this story tell you about how archaeology works?

lessons.title: Who Was Mithras?
lessons.mainIdea: Mithras was a god worshipped in secret by small groups of men across the Roman Empire, and his main picture shows him holding down a bull.
reading: About 1,900 years ago, some men in Roman towns met in secret to worship a god called *Mithras*. In pictures, Mithras is a young man. He wears a soft, pointed cap and a cape that flies out behind him. The most famous scene shows him holding down a bull.

This bull scene was in almost every meeting place. Two helpers with torches stand beside Mithras. One holds his torch up. The other holds his torch down. The Sun and the Moon often watch from above. Members knew what the scene meant. They did not write it down for us.

The name Mithra came from Persia, a land far to the east. But scholars disagree about how much of this religion came from Persia. Many now think it was mostly made in the Roman world, using a Persian name. This is a *debate*, and it is not settled.

words.d: a god worshipped in secret by small groups of men in the Roman Empire
a discussion where people who study a question give different answers and reasons

look.title: Reading a Carved Scene
look.text: Picture a stone carving. In the middle, a young man in a pointed cap kneels on a bull. His cape blows out behind him. On the left, a helper holds a torch up high. On the right, another helper holds a torch pointing down. In the top corners are a sun and a moon.
look.prompt: The two torches point in opposite directions. What might up and down stand for? Remember that nobody knows for sure.

check.q: What does the most famous picture of Mithras show?
check.why: The reading says the most famous scene shows Mithras holding down a bull.

check.q: How do the two helpers in the bull scene hold their torches?
choices: One holds a torch up and one holds a torch down
check.why: In the scene, one helper holds his torch up and the other holds it down.

check.q: What is the debate about Mithras?
choices: How much of the religion came from Persia
check.why: Scholars disagree about how much came from Persia; many think it was mostly made in the Roman world.

lessons.title: A Room Like a Cave
lessons.mainIdea: Followers of Mithras met in small, dark, cave-like rooms called mithraea, where they shared a meal together.
reading: A meeting place for Mithras is called a *mithraeum*. More than one are called mithraea. Many were built underground or in dark rooms with no windows. Members wanted the room to feel like a cave. In their story, Mithras killed the bull in a cave.

Most mithraea were long and narrow. A raised bench ran down each side. Members lay or sat on the benches to share a *ritual meal*, a meal eaten as part of worship. At the far end was the bull scene, often lit by lamps. Most rooms held only a few dozen people.

The members left no holy book behind. So how do we know all this? We learn from the rooms, the carvings and paintings, and words carved on altars. We also learn from writers who did not like the religion. Each kind of clue tells part of the story.

words.d: a small, cave-like room where followers of Mithras met; more than one are called mithraea
a meal eaten together as part of worship

look.title: Step Inside
look.text: Picture going down a few stone steps. The air is cool. The room has no windows. Along both long walls are raised benches, like wide stone beds. Oil lamps flicker. At the far end, lamplight shines on a carving of Mithras and the bull.
look.prompt: How is this room different from a big temple with columns in the sunlight? Why might a small group want a room like this?

check.q: What is a mithraeum?
choices: A small, cave-like room where followers of Mithras met
check.why: A mithraeum is a small, cave-like meeting room for followers of Mithras.

check.q: What were the benches along the walls used for?
check.why: Members lay or sat on the benches to share a ritual meal.

check.q: Since there is no holy book, how do we learn about Mithras?
choices: From the rooms, carvings, altar words and outside writers
From a book written by Mithras
check.why: The reading lists the rooms, carvings, paintings, altar words and writers who did not like the religion.

lessons.title: Soldiers, Traders and Workers
lessons.mainIdea: Only men joined Mithras groups, and they included soldiers, traders, officials and even enslaved men, from Britain to Syria.
reading: Most scholars agree that only men joined the groups of Mithras. Many were Roman soldiers. Others were traders, government workers and enslaved or freed men. Inside the mithraeum, rich and poor members ate together at the same benches.

Mithraea have been found across the Roman Empire. They stretch from Britain in the west to Syria in the east. Soldiers moved from place to place. So did each *merchant*, a person who buys and sells goods. They seem to have carried the religion with them.

One mithraeum in Syria has a carved date. Archers from the Roman army set it up around 168 CE. This kind of carved writing is called an *inscription*. Inscriptions help us know who the members were and when they met.

words.d: a person who buys and sells goods, often traveling to do it
words carved or written on stone, metal or another hard surface

look.title: A Soldier Pushes Away a Crown
look.text: In a cave, a new soldier of Mithras is offered a crown on the tip of a sword. He is taught to push it off his head and say that Mithras is his only crown. After that, he never wears a crown again.
look.cite: Tertullian, The Chaplet (De Corona), chapter 15, about 200 CE; retold from the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation
look.prompt: Tertullian was a Christian writer who did not like this religion. What does his story tell us? Why should we read it with care?

check.q: Who could join the groups of Mithras?
check.why: Most scholars agree that only men joined the groups of Mithras.

check.q: What is an inscription?
choices: A painting on a cave wall
A song sung at a meal
Words carved on a hard surface
check.why: An inscription is words carved or written on stone, metal or another hard surface.

check.q: How did the religion of Mithras likely spread so far?
choices: Soldiers and merchants carried it as they moved
A king ordered everyone to join
check.why: The reading says soldiers and merchants moved from place to place and seem to have carried the religion.

lessons.title: Under a Church in Rome
lessons.mainIdea: Beneath the church of San Clemente in Rome, digging revealed layers of history, with a mithraeum near the bottom.
reading: San Clemente is a church in Rome. The church you walk into today was built in the 1100s. In 1857, an Irish priest named Joseph Mullooly began to dig beneath it. He found an older church underneath, from the 300s.

Below that church were even older Roman buildings. In 1867, the diggers found a mithraeum down there. It had been built in the early 200s. But water kept flooding the lowest *layer*. A tunnel to drain the water was finished in 1914. Only then could the mithraeum be fully dug out.

Today, visitors walk down stairs through three layers of time. At the bottom, they can see the benches and the altar of Mithras. They can still hear water running nearby. Digging carefully to study the past like this is called an *excavation*.

words.d: one level of something that lies on top of or under another level
careful digging to find and study things from the past

look.title: Layers Under San Clemente
look.cite: Mithraeum of San Clemente, Mithraeum.eu database; Basilica of San Clemente, Rome
look.prompt: Which layer is the oldest? Why does the oldest layer end up at the bottom?

check.q: Who began digging under San Clemente in 1857?
check.why: The Irish priest Joseph Mullooly began to dig beneath the church in 1857.

check.q: Why could the mithraeum not be fully dug out until 1914?
choices: The church would not allow it
Water kept flooding the lowest layer
check.why: Water flooded the lowest layer until a drainage tunnel was finished in 1914.

check.q: What is an excavation?
choices: Careful digging to study the past
check.why: The reading says digging carefully to study the past is called an excavation.

lessons.title: The Floor at Ostia
lessons.mainIdea: A mosaic floor in a mithraeum at Ostia shows the seven grades, or ranks, of the members of Mithras.
reading: Ostia was the port city of ancient Rome, near the mouth of the river Tiber. Ships brought grain and goods there. Many mithraea have been found in Ostia. One of them is named for a man called Felicissimus.

In 1940, archaeologists Guido and Raissa Calza dug up this mithraeum. It was built in the second half of the 200s CE. Its floor is a *mosaic*, a picture made of many tiny pieces of stone set close together.

The mosaic is divided into seven panels, one after another. Each panel stands for one *grade*, or rank, of members. Each has its own symbols and its own planet. An eighth panel names Felicissimus. It is like a ladder that members climbed, step by step.

words.d: a picture made of many small pieces of stone or glass set close together
a rank or level in a group; members move up from one grade to the next

look.title: A Ladder on the Floor
look.text: Picture a long, narrow floor made of tiny black and white stones. It is divided into boxes, one after another, like the rungs of a ladder. Each box holds small pictures, such as a cup, a torch or a moon. As you walk toward the far end of the room, you walk up the ladder.
look.prompt: Why might a group put its ranks on the floor, where members walk over them? What would that feel like?

check.q: What was Ostia?
choices: The port city of ancient Rome
check.why: Ostia was the port city of ancient Rome, near the mouth of the river Tiber.

check.q: What is a mosaic?
choices: A picture made of many tiny pieces of stone
check.why: A mosaic is a picture made of many small pieces of stone or glass set close together.

check.q: How many grades are shown on the Felicissimus floor?
check.why: The mosaic has seven panels, one for each grade, plus an eighth that names Felicissimus.

lessons.title: Seven Steps Up
lessons.mainIdea: Members of Mithras climbed seven grades, from Raven to Father, and each grade was linked to a planet.
reading: Other evidence agrees with the floor at Ostia. There were seven grades. In order, they were Raven, Bridegroom, Soldier, Lion, Persian, Runner of the Sun, and Father. The Father was the highest grade. He led the group.

Each grade had a *planet*. Romans counted seven moving lights in the sky as planets, including the Sun and the Moon. The Raven went with Mercury. The Soldier went with Mars. The Persian went with the Moon. The Runner of the Sun went with the Sun. The Father went with Saturn.

What did members do to move up a grade? We do not know for sure. The members kept that secret, and few clues survive. The grades show one clear idea, though. Belonging to the group meant growing, one step at a time.

words.d: to the Romans, one of seven moving lights in the sky, including the Sun and the Moon
a person's level or position in a group

look.title: Design Your Own Ladder
look.text: The Mithras groups named their seven steps after animals and people: Raven, Bridegroom, Soldier, Lion, Persian, Runner of the Sun and Father. Imagine a club that helps people learn to be kind. It has seven steps. Each step needs a name and a small picture.
look.prompt: Name your seven steps and draw a symbol for each. What would someone learn at each step?

check.q: What was the highest grade in the groups of Mithras?
check.why: The Father was the highest grade and led the group.

check.q: Which grade went with the planet Mars?
check.why: The reading says the Soldier went with Mars.

check.q: What do we know about how members moved up a grade?
choices: We do not know for sure
check.why: The members kept it secret, and few clues survive, so we do not know for sure.

lessons.title: The Head in the Mud
lessons.mainIdea: The London Mithraeum, found in 1954, drew huge crowds and was later rebuilt so people can visit it today.
reading: The London Mithraeum was built around the middle of the 200s CE. It stood near a small river called the Walbrook. Over hundreds of years, it was buried under mud and newer buildings. People forgot it was there.

In 1954, archaeologists W. F. Grimes and Audrey Williams dug at the site. On 18 September, the last planned day of the dig, they found the marble head of Mithras. Long lines of people came to see the temple. Many people argued that it should be saved.

The stones were moved and put back together nearby. Later, the temple was rebuilt again, on the spot where it was first found. It opened to visitors in 2017. When people build something again from its old parts, we say they *reconstruct* it.

words.d: to build something again, often from its old parts
a hard, smooth stone often used for statues

look.title: The London Mithraeum Over Time
look.cite: John D. Shepherd, The Temple of Mithras, London: Excavations by W. F. Grimes and A. Williams at the Walbrook, English Heritage, 1998; London Mithraeum Bloomberg SPACE, 2017
look.prompt: About how many years passed between when the temple was built and when the head was found?

check.q: What was found on 18 September 1954?
check.why: On the last planned day of the dig, the team found the marble head of Mithras.

check.q: What does reconstruct mean?
choices: To build something again from its old parts
check.why: To reconstruct is to build something again, often from its old parts, as London did with the temple.

check.q: When did the rebuilt London Mithraeum open to visitors?
check.why: The reading says it opened to visitors in 2017.

lessons.title: A Teacher Comes to Croton
lessons.mainIdea: Pythagoras, a Greek thinker from Samos, led a brotherhood of followers in southern Italy about 2,500 years ago.
reading: *Pythagoras* was born on Samos, a Greek island, more than 2,500 years ago. As a grown man, he moved west to a Greek city called Croton. Croton is in southern Italy. Many Greeks lived in cities there.

In Croton, Pythagoras became a teacher. People came to learn from him and to live by his rules. His followers formed a *brotherhood*, a close group who treat each other like family. Later writers say some women were followers, too. Many shared their meals and their way of life.
Pythagoras wrote no books that survive. His followers were called Pythagoreans. They studied numbers, music and how to live a good life. They kept some of their teachings inside the group.

words.d: a Greek thinker from Samos who led a brotherhood in southern Italy about 2,500 years ago
a close group of people who treat each other like family and share rules
a person who learns from a leader and lives by that leader's ideas

look.title: From an Island to Italy
look.text: Picture a map. In the east, near the coast of what is now Turkey, is a small Greek island called Samos. Far to the west, across the sea, is the toe of Italy's boot. On the sole of that boot is the city of Croton. Pythagoras made that long trip.
look.prompt: Trace the trip with your finger. Why might a teacher move to a new city to start a group?

check.q: Where was Pythagoras born?
check.why: The reading says Pythagoras was born on Samos, a Greek island.

check.q: What is a brotherhood?
choices: A close group who treat each other like family
check.why: A brotherhood is a close group of people who treat each other like family.

check.q: What did the Pythagoreans study?
choices: Numbers, music and how to live a good life
check.why: The reading says they studied numbers, music and how to live a good life.

lessons.title: Rules and Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Later writers say the Pythagoreans lived by short rules and that new members first had to listen in silence.
reading: Later writers describe strict rules for the brotherhood. They say new members had to stay silent for a long time, some say five years. They listened and learned before they could speak in the group. This kind of silence is a way to show *discipline*, or self-control.

The group also had short sayings to live by. People called them things heard, because members learned them by listening. One famous rule was: do not eat beans. Even in ancient times, people argued about why. Nobody is sure today.

A Roman writer, Cicero, said Pythagoreans ended arguments with a short phrase: He himself said it. That meant Pythagoras had said so, so the matter was closed. Some people admired this *loyalty*. Others thought people should give reasons, not just names.

words.d: self-control; following rules even when it is hard
staying true and faithful to a person or group

look.title: Short Rules to Live By
look.text: Among the rules of Pythagoras: do not stir a fire with a knife. Do not step over a scale for weighing. Stay away from beans.
look.cite: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 8, about 230 CE; retold from the translation by R. D. Hicks, 1925
look.prompt: These rules sound strange. Many people think some were meant as picture-sayings with hidden meanings. What might do not stir a fire with a knife mean?

check.q: According to later writers, what did new members do at first?
check.why: Later writers say new members stayed silent for a long time and listened before they spoke.

check.q: What is discipline?
choices: Self-control, following rules even when it is hard
check.why: The reading says discipline is self-control.

check.q: What did the phrase He himself said it mean to Pythagoreans?
choices: Pythagoras had said so, so the matter was closed
check.why: Cicero said Pythagoreans used the phrase to show that Pythagoras had said so, closing the argument.

lessons.title: Numbers Everywhere
lessons.mainIdea: Pythagoreans believed numbers could explain the world, from music to shapes, though some ideas named for Pythagoras are older than him.
reading: The Pythagoreans believed numbers were the key to the whole world. They studied music this way. A shorter string plays a higher note. A string half as long plays a note that sounds the same, only higher. We call that an octave. The two lengths make a *ratio* of 2 to 1.

You may meet the Pythagorean theorem in math class. It is about a *right triangle*, a triangle with one square corner. Square the two short sides and add them. You get the square of the long side. For sides 3 and 4, that is 9 plus 16, which makes 25, or 5 times 5.

But the theorem is older than Pythagoras. A clay tablet from ancient Babylon, called Plimpton 322, lists number sets that fit this rule. It was made more than a thousand years before him. Nobody knows if Pythagoras himself proved the rule.

words.d: a way to compare two numbers, such as 2 to 1
a triangle with one square corner, like the corner of a book

look.title: The 3-4-5 Triangle
look.cite: Euclid, Elements, Book 1, Proposition 47, about 300 BCE
look.prompt: Add the first two numbers. What do you get? Try it with sides 6, 8 and 10.

check.q: What is a right triangle?
choices: A triangle with three equal sides
A triangle with one square corner
A triangle drawn on a floor
check.why: The reading says a right triangle has one square corner.

check.q: In a 3-4-5 triangle, what is 9 plus 16?
check.why: 9 plus 16 makes 25, which is 5 times 5, the square of the long side.

check.q: What does the tablet Plimpton 322 show?
choices: The rule was known in Babylon long before Pythagoras
The rule was invented in London
check.why: Plimpton 322, from ancient Babylon, lists number sets that fit the rule more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.

lessons.title: What We Know and What We Were Told
lessons.mainIdea: Most stories about Pythagoras were written hundreds of years after he died, so historians sort them into likely facts and legends.
reading: Most of what we read about Pythagoras was written 600 to 800 years after he lived. Writers such as Iamblichus, around 300 CE, collected old stories. Some stories may be true. Others grew bigger with each telling. A story that is told for a long time but cannot be proven is a *legend*.

One legend says a member named Hippasus shared a math secret with outsiders. In the story, the group punished him. Historians treat this as a legend. It comes only from late writers, and no earlier record backs it up.

Some things are better supported. The historian Polybius wrote in the 100s BCE that Pythagorean meeting places in southern Italy were burned. So the group seems to have faced real anger from its neighbors. But even Polybius wrote hundreds of years later, and the dates are still debated. Historians call a source written long after the events a *late source*.

words.d: a story told for a long time that cannot be proven true
a source written long after the events it describes

look.title: Sort the Stories
look.text: Card A: Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos. Card B: A member named Hippasus was punished for sharing a math secret. Card C: Polybius wrote that Pythagorean meeting places were burned. Card D: A Babylonian tablet shows the triangle rule is older than Pythagoras.
look.prompt: Sort the cards into two piles: well supported, or legend. Explain one choice using the reading.

check.q: About how long after Pythagoras did writers like Iamblichus live?
check.why: The reading says most stories were written 600 to 800 years after Pythagoras lived.

check.q: Why do historians treat the Hippasus story as a legend?
choices: It comes only from late writers with no earlier record
It is carved on a mosaic
check.why: The story comes only from late writers, and no earlier record backs it up.

check.q: What did Polybius write about the Pythagoreans?
choices: Their meeting places in southern Italy were burned
They built the church of San Clemente
check.why: Polybius wrote that Pythagorean meeting places in southern Italy were burned.

review.q: What is the name for a meeting room of Mithras?
review.why: A mithraeum is the small, cave-like room where followers of Mithras met.

review.q: Which list shows the first and last of the seven grades of Mithras?
review.why: The grades went from Raven, the lowest, up to Father, the highest.

review.q: Which place has a mosaic floor showing the seven grades?
review.why: The Felicissimus mithraeum at Ostia, dug up in 1940, has the seven-grade mosaic.

review.q: Where was the marble head of Mithras found in 1954?
review.why: The head was found on the last day of the Walbrook dig in London.

review.q: How were the Mithras groups and the Pythagoreans alike?
choices: Both kept some things inside the group
review.why: Mithras members kept their rites secret, and Pythagoreans kept some teachings inside the group.

review.q: How did the Mithras groups and the Pythagoreans differ in who could join?
choices: Only men joined Mithras; later writers say some women followed Pythagoras
review.why: Most scholars agree only men joined Mithras, while later writers say some women followed Pythagoras.

review.q: Which source was written by someone who did not like the religion of Mithras?
choices: An altar inscription by army archers
Tertullian's story of the soldier's crown
review.why: Tertullian was a Christian writer who opposed the religion, so we read his story with care.

review.q: Why do historians sort stories about Pythagoras carefully?
choices: Most were written hundreds of years after he lived
He wrote a diary every day
They were all carved on floors
review.why: Most stories come from late sources, written 600 to 800 years later, so some are legends.
